body:
Private-equity firms Clayton, Dubilier & Rice (CD&R) and GTCR have jointly approached Global Payments (NYSE: GPN) with a bid to take the card-processing giant private in a leveraged buyout (LBO) valuing the company at approximately $40 billion in enterprise value, the Financial Times reported on October 30, 2026. Reuters independently confirmed the approach the same afternoon, citing a source familiar with the deal.

The disclosure sent Global Payments shares surging more than 11 percent in afternoon trading — their best single-day performance in over eight months — closing at $96.84 and briefly erasing months of investor frustration over a company that has become one of the most contentious names in fintech.

If the deal closes at the reported enterprise value, it would rank as the third-largest leveraged buyout ever executed — trailing only Electronic Arts' $55 billion privatization, which closed in August 2026 and stands as the all-time record, and the 2007 buyout of Texas utility TXU at $45 billion. The GPN bid would test leveraged-finance markets' appetite for an unprecedented debt load on top of a balance sheet already burdened by the January 2026 Worldpay acquisition.

Deal Mechanics: Equity, Two Debt Numbers, and Why Both Matter

The $40 billion headline figure reflects Global Payments' full enterprise value: a market capitalization that surged to approximately $25.6 billion after the news broke, plus approximately $17 billion in net debt, according to LSEG data cited by multiple outlets.

Those two figures require a brief reconciliation, because the draft discussion on Wall Street has used a different, equally legitimate number: analysts at William Blair and in multiple SEC-filed disclosures cite approximately $22 billion in gross debt on Global Payments' books — reflecting the full outstanding principal on the company's unsecured notes and revolving credit facilities. The gap between $17 billion and $22 billion represents roughly $5 billion in cash and cash equivalents that Global Payments holds against those obligations. Net debt subtracts cash; gross debt does not. Both figures matter to an LBO buyer, but for different reasons: net debt determines enterprise value; gross debt determines the debt-service obligations the new owners must manage from day one.

In a leveraged buyout, acquirers typically pile additional borrowed money on top of existing obligations — meaning credit markets would need to absorb a total debt load that analysts at William Blair pegged at "nearly $22 billion before any new acquisition financing." In a research note published Friday, William Blair called the potential bid "credible" given GTCR's existing position in Global Payments, but flagged the debt pile as a significant hurdle — "especially in a rising rate environment."

B. Riley equivocated less. The firm, which carries a Street-high $194 price target on the stock and an unchanged Buy rating, said the bid underscored that Global Payments is "materially mispriced," laying out a range of private-equity outcomes spanning from $84 to $190 per share depending on deal structure and leverage assumptions.

Mizuho analyst Dan Dolev was more sanguine still, writing in a note to clients that he was "not surprised" by the potential bid, citing the widening gap between how public and private markets have been valuing legacy payment processors. With Global Payments trading near a decade-low before news broke, that gap had become especially pronounced.

Who Is Bidding — and Why This Pair Makes Strategic Sense

Clayton, Dubilier & Rice (CD&R) is a New York-based private equity firm founded in 1978, originally as a turnaround management investment firm and known today for large-scale operational-improvement investments across business services, healthcare, industrials, and financial services. It ranks among the world's top-fifteen largest PE firms by assets and has completed over $140 billion in aggregate deal value across its history.

CD&R is not primarily known as a payments specialist, but its appetite for large-scale carve-outs and public-to-private transactions is well-documented: its November 2025 acquisition of Sealed Air for $10.3 billion in enterprise value was among the largest buyouts of that year and is consistent with a pattern of mega-deal appetite. Reports indicate CD&R is currently raising a flagship fund of approximately $26 billion — a war chest that would make a $40 billion co-investment structurally feasible.

GTCR private equity firm, the Chicago-based firm founded in 1980, is the more payments-seasoned half of the partnership — and arguably the more strategically motivated. GTCR invested in Transaction Network Services (2002), recapitalized secure-payment provider VeriFone (2002), and built Paya Holdings into an integrated-payments platform before selling it to Nuvei in January 2023 for approximately $1.3 billion.

The Worldpay chapter, however, is what makes GTCR's role in this bid particularly compelling. GTCR acquired a 55 percent controlling stake in Worldpay from Fidelity National Information Services (FIS) in July 2023 at an $18.5 billion valuation, rebuilt the business over roughly two years, and then sold that stake to Global Payments in January 2026 as part of a three-way, $24.25 billion transaction — receiving approximately $6 billion in cash and 42.8 million shares of Global Payments stock as consideration. That stock position, representing roughly 15 percent of Global Payments' equity capitalization, made GTCR the company's largest outside shareholder virtually overnight.

GTCR's motivation in the reported buyout bid is therefore unmistakable: the firm bought Worldpay cheaply from a struggling parent, turned it around in roughly two years, and sold it at a significant markup — but in doing so became a large, illiquid shareholder of a publicly listed company whose stock then declined further. A take-private, if it succeeded, would allow GTCR to effectively re-privatize the combined entity and pursue the same operational-improvement playbook on a much larger canvas.

A Stock in Freefall: How Global Payments Got Here

Global Payments announced its intention to acquire Worldpay from GTCR and FIS in April 2025, in a complex three-way transaction valued at $24.25 billion. Under the deal's structure, Global Payments paid approximately $6 billion in cash and issued 42.8 million shares to GTCR for its controlling stake, while simultaneously selling its Issuer Solutions business to FIS for $13.5 billion — a division swap designed to transform Global Payments into a pure-play merchant-acquiring business serving more than 6 million customers across 175 countries, processing some $3.7 trillion in annual payment volume.

Wall Street's reaction was swift and severe. Shares plunged 17 percent on the announcement day, briefly touching their lowest level in a decade, as analysts questioned the strategic rationale and the financial risk. TD Cowen downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold, warning that the acquisition "adds complexity, leverage, and increased execution risk that runs counter to needed simplification." Jefferies and KBW followed with similar downgrades.

The market backlash partly reflected a perceived contradiction: Global Payments had previously signaled a focus on divestitures and capital returns to shareholders, only to pivot to a $24 billion acquisition that increased net leverage and reversed recent debt-reduction progress. The Worldpay deal, analysts noted, bore little resemblance to the simplification story management had been selling. By the time the acquisition formally closed in January 2026, Global Payments stock had fallen more than 60 percent from its all-time high set in 2021.

It was not the only restructuring happening inside the company. Between early 2024 and September 2024 — before the Worldpay deal even closed — Global Payments laid off approximately 5,400 employees across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, India, and other markets, as the company worked to streamline its cost structure. The layoffs underscore that Global Payments entered the Worldpay integration already in cost-reduction mode, a fact that any PE buyer would factor into projections — as a source of further achievable cuts, or as evidence that the easy reductions have already been taken.

The stock decline attracted activist attention. Elliott Investment Management — one of the world's most formidable corporate agitators, managing roughly $80 billion in assets — quietly built a significant stake in Global Payments in mid-2025, weeks after the Worldpay deal was announced. In September 2025, Global Payments and Elliott reached a cooperation agreement, with the company appointing two independent directors mutually agreed upon with Elliott: Patricia Watson, a payments-technology veteran with prior executive roles at TSYS and NCR Atleos and board seats at Southwest Airlines and Rockwell Automation; and Archana Deskus, a former CTO at PayPal who also serves on the boards of Cognizant and East West Bancorp. A third Elliott-linked board appointment was agreed for the 2026 annual meeting.

The board additions improved investor confidence somewhat, but could not fully stabilize the stock. As of October 30, Global Payments was still trading near its ten-year lows — creating exactly the kind of depressed-valuation opportunity that private equity firms exist to exploit.

The Debt Problem: Why the Numbers Are Harder Than They Look

The single biggest obstacle to any deal is the same one that has weighed on Global Payments in public markets: the company's debt load. The Worldpay acquisition was partly financed by $7.7 billion in newly issued debt, and including Worldpay's legacy obligations, Global Payments entered 2026 carrying approximately $22 billion in gross outstanding debt — roughly six times its adjusted EBITDA by some analyst estimates.

This is the structural challenge that separates this potential LBO from a routine take-private. In a standard leveraged buyout, the acquiring consortium adds a new layer of debt on top of the target's existing obligations, using the target's projected cash flows as collateral. The debt is then serviced and, over the typical four-to-seven-year holding period, paid down — ideally leaving the company in condition for an eventual re-listing or strategic sale at a higher valuation.

The math works when the company generates strong, predictable free cash flow. Global Payments has projected adjusted free cash flow exceeding $4 billion in 2027 and $5 billion in 2028, along with a target to bring net leverage to approximately 3x by the end of 2027. Those projections, if credible, would support debt service on a large LBO package. But they also assume a smooth Worldpay integration — which public-market investors have been skeptical of — and a revenue growth trajectory that the company's recent guidance revisions have complicated.

History offers a caution here. Paul Volcker warned in 1984 of "top-heavy reversed pyramids of debt" in the early LBO era. More recently, Moody's has documented that PE-backed companies are twice as likely to default as non-PE-backed companies. And the bank financing that would fund a $40 billion buyout would need to compete with memory of what happened to other highly leveraged payment-sector names when credit conditions tightened. None of these historical patterns make the deal impossible — but they explain why William Blair's analysts placed the deal odds "well below 50 percent" in their Friday note.

A representative from CD&R declined to comment. GTCR also declined to comment. Global Payments did not respond to requests for comment from Reuters, the Financial Times, or other outlets. The Financial Times noted explicitly that the talks are ongoing and may not result in a deal.
